title: Scale containers in Azure Container Apps

questions.q: A gRPC service keeps long-lived connections open, and the team wants it to scale with load and drop to zero overnight. Which rule type fits best?

options.text: CPU scale rule
options.why: CPU rules can't scale to zero.

options.text: Memory scale rule
options.why: Memory rules can't scale to zero.

options.text: HTTP scale rule
options.why: HTTP rules suit short request-response cycles; Learn prefers TCP for gRPC.

options.text: TCP scale rule
options.why: Correct. TCP rules suit WebSockets, gRPC and long-lived connections, and support scale to zero.

questions.hint: Long-lived connections aren't counted well as requests. Which rule counts open connections?
questions.explain: TCP scaling counts concurrent connections and supports scale to zero.

questions.q: What is the default HTTP concurrency threshold per replica in Azure Container Apps?

options.text: 1 request
options.why: Learn gives a higher default.

options.text: 100 requests
options.why: 100 appears in Learn's combined-rule YAML, not as the default.

options.text: 50 requests
options.why: 50 is the custom value in Learn's example command.

options.text: 10 requests
options.why: Correct. The default HTTP concurrency threshold is 10 requests per replica.

questions.hint: The default HTTP concurrency threshold is a small round number.
questions.explain: The default is 10 concurrent requests per replica; adjust it to the app's capacity.

questions.q: A background processor has ingress disabled, no minimum replicas and no custom scale rule. After the first idle period it never starts again. Why?

options.text: It scaled to zero and has no trigger to activate it
options.why: Correct. With ingress disabled and no minimum or rule, the app scales to zero and can't restart.

options.text: CPU rules polled every 30 seconds can't see a stopped app
options.why: There's no CPU rule configured in this scenario.

options.text: The 300-second cool-down repeats until a revision is deployed
options.why: The cool-down applies once before scaling to zero.

options.text: Jobs can't use HTTP rules, so the app was converted to a job
options.why: The app isn't a job; the problem is the missing trigger.

questions.hint: Nothing can wake an app with no ingress, no minimum and no event rule.
questions.explain: Set a minimum of one replica or add an event-driven rule that can wake the app.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. An app has `minReplicas: 0`, a CPU rule at 70% and no other rules.

rows.text: The app can scale to zero when CPU usage is low.
rows.why: CPU rules need a running replica to measure utilization, so they keep at least one.

rows.text: The platform checks the CPU rule every 30 seconds.
rows.why: Custom scalers such as CPU and memory are polled every 30 seconds.

rows.text: Adding an HTTP rule as well would let the app scale to zero.
rows.why: Combine resource rules with HTTP or event rules for scale to zero.

questions.hint: CPU and memory need a running replica to measure. Think about what happens at zero.
questions.explain: CPU and memory rules always keep at least one replica; pair them with HTTP or event rules to reach zero.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. An app scales from 1 replica under a sudden sustained load spike, with a maximum of 30.

rows.text: The platform waits 300 seconds before starting to scale up.
rows.why: The scale-up stabilization window is zero seconds.

rows.text: Scale-up proceeds in steps such as 1, 4, 8, 16, then the maximum.
rows.why: Scale-up doubles in steps until it reaches the maximum.

rows.text: When load ends, replicas are removed one at a time over five minutes.
rows.why: After the 300-second window, all replicas that need to shut down are removed at once.

rows.text: With an HTTP rule and a CPU rule, either one exceeding its threshold scales the app out.
rows.why: With multiple rules, the app scales out when any rule's threshold is met.

questions.hint: Scale-up doesn't wait; scale-down does. Any rule can trigger a scale-out.
questions.explain: Scale up immediately in doubling steps; scale down after 300 seconds, all at once; any rule can trigger scale out.

questions.q: A Service Bus scale rule has messageCount set to 5, and 50 messages are waiting in the queue. How many replicas does the scaler request?

options.why: That's one replica per message.
The scaler divides, it doesn't multiply.
That would be one replica per 10 messages.
Correct. 50 ÷ 5 = 10 replicas.

questions.hint: The Service Bus scaler divides the waiting messages by the threshold.
questions.explain: The Service Bus scaler divides the active message count by messageCount.

questions.q: A document-extraction worker scales with a Service Bus KEDA rule. Its CPU sits at 90% while the queue is empty, and the team asks whether CPU affects the replica count. Which value does the Service Bus scaler use?

options.text: The CPU utilization of each replica
options.why: CPU is a separate rule type. The Service Bus scaler looks at the queue.

options.text: The number of open AMQP connections
options.why: Connections aren't the scaling signal. Queued messages are.

options.text: The namespace's total size in bytes
options.why: Storage size doesn't indicate how much work is waiting.

options.text: The queue's active message count
options.why: Correct. The Service Bus scaler uses the active message count divided by messageCount.

questions.hint: An event-driven scaler watches the event source, not the replicas.
questions.explain: The Service Bus scaler divides the active message count by messageCount to calculate the desired replica count. It's independent of CPU.

questions.q: An Event Hub has 32 partitions, and the processing app's scale rule allows up to 100 replicas. What should you expect?

options.text: Each replica reads every partition, so 100 replicas triple throughput
options.why: Within a consumer group, a partition has one active reader.

options.text: The scaler is rejected because maxReplicas exceeds 32
options.why: Learn says it provides no benefit; it doesn't say the rule is rejected.

options.text: Up to 100 replicas share the load evenly across partitions
options.why: Each partition can be read by one consumer at a time within a consumer group.

options.text: Replicas beyond 32 add no extra processing benefit
options.why: Correct. You can't benefit from more replicas than partitions.

questions.hint: Each partition can be read by one consumer in a group at a time.
questions.explain: Partition count caps effective parallelism for Event Hubs (and Kafka).

questions.q: A simple thumbnail queue needs no sessions, dead-letter queues or scheduled messages, and cost matters. Which scaler and threshold should you use?

options.text: Azure Service Bus scaler with messageCount
options.why: Service Bus suits workloads that need advanced features or higher throughput.

options.text: Azure Storage Queue scaler with queueLength
options.why: Correct. Storage Queue is the simpler, lower-cost option for basic queues; queueLength is its threshold.

options.text: A CPU scale rule with a 70% threshold
options.why: A CPU rule can't scale to zero and doesn't track the queue.

options.text: Azure Event Hubs scaler with unprocessedEventThreshold
options.why: Event Hubs is for partitioned, high-throughput streams.

questions.hint: No sessions, no dead-lettering, and cost matters. Which queue service is simpler?
questions.explain: Use Storage Queue scaling for straightforward queue processing; Service Bus for sessions, DLQs, scheduled messages or higher throughput.

questions.q: A Service Bus processor's queue depth keeps growing faster than replicas are added, and the team stores the namespace connection string as a secret. Which two changes follow Learn's best practices? (Select two.)

options.text: Switch the rule to a memory scale rule
options.why: Memory rules don't track the backlog and can't scale to zero.

options.text: Lower the messageCount threshold
options.why: Correct. If depth grows faster than replicas scale, lower the threshold.

options.text: Use a user-assigned managed identity with Azure Service Bus Data Receiver
options.why: Correct. Prefer managed identity over stored connection strings in production.

options.text: Raise messageCount so each replica processes more messages at once
options.why: messageCount is target queue depth per replica, not processing concurrency; raising it slows scaling.

questions.hint: Grow replicas sooner, and stop storing a connection string.
questions.explain: Tune messageCount from measured capacity and queue delay, and authenticate scalers with managed identity.

questions.q: A Kafka scale rule has lagThreshold set to 100, and the consumer group's lag across all partitions is 500 messages. The topic has 10 partitions. How many replicas does the scaler target?

options.why: Correct. 500 messages of lag divided by a lagThreshold of 100 gives 5 replicas.
That would be the lag divided by the partition count, which isn't how the scaler works.

options.text: 10, one per partition
options.why: The partition count caps useful parallelism, but the calculation divides lag by the threshold.
100 is the threshold itself, not the desired replica count.

questions.hint: Divide the total lag by the lag that one replica is expected to handle.
questions.explain: lagThreshold sets the lag that triggers scaling. With lagThreshold 100 and 500 messages of lag, the scaler targets 5 replicas (up to the partition count).

questions.q: Match each KEDA ScaledObject field to its Container Apps equivalent.

items.why: Credentials become Container Apps secrets referenced in --scale-rule-auth.

questions.hint: Container Apps has CLI flags that map to KEDA ScaledObject fields one to one.
questions.explain: Container Apps doesn't support the full TriggerAuthentication resource; reference secrets directly in the rule.

questions.q: From 8 AM to 6 PM on weekdays, an API needs at least five replicas ready, and it must still react to unexpected spikes and scale to zero at night. What should you configure?

options.text: A cron scaler alone with desiredReplicas set to the maximum
options.why: Cron alone can't react to unexpected spikes and wastes capacity.

options.text: A cron scaler with desiredReplicas 5, plus an HTTP scale rule
options.why: Correct. Cron sets baseline capacity in the window; HTTP handles spikes; the highest count wins and it can reach zero at night.

options.text: minReplicas 5 with no rules, so capacity stays available
options.why: A fixed minimum of 5 never scales to zero at night.

options.text: A Prometheus scaler that queries the time of day
options.why: Prometheus scales on metric values, not scheduled windows.

questions.hint: Combine a schedule with a reactive rule. Container Apps uses the highest replica count among active scalers.
questions.explain: Combine scheduled (cron) and reactive (HTTP or event) scaling; Container Apps uses the highest replica count among active scalers.

questions.q: Workers pull tasks from Redis, and sometimes a worker crashes after taking a task but before finishing it. Which scaler accounts for this in-progress work?

options.text: Cron scaler, so capacity is fixed during the busy window
options.why: Cron doesn't look at the work at all.

options.text: Redis Streams scaler, which tracks pending entries for a consumer group
options.why: Correct. Streams scaling tracks delivered-but-unacknowledged entries, so it handles failures better.

options.text: Redis Lists scaler, because LLEN counts in-progress items
options.why: LLEN counts queued items; it doesn't track work already taken.

options.text: Kafka scaler, using lagThreshold on the Redis list
options.why: The Kafka scaler reads Kafka consumer lag, not Redis.

questions.hint: One Redis scaler knows about entries that were taken but not yet acknowledged.
questions.explain: Redis Streams scalers consider work in progress (pending entries), not just queued work.

questions.q: An inference API's real load is best described by an application metric, pending tokens per second, which it already exposes to a Prometheus server. HTTP concurrency doesn't reflect the actual work. Which scaler fits?

options.text: A CPU scale rule at 50%
options.why: CPU is only an indirect signal, and the team already has a direct metric.

options.text: A cron scaler with a fixed replica count
options.why: A schedule doesn't react to the metric at all.

options.text: The Prometheus scaler with a PromQL query and a threshold
options.why: Correct. Prometheus scaling uses application-specific metrics, and the scaler divides the query result by the threshold.

options.text: An HTTP scale rule with a lower concurrency threshold
options.why: Changing the threshold still scales on concurrency, which you said doesn't reflect the work.

questions.hint: When standard signals don't describe the work, scale on the custom metric you already collect.
questions.explain: Prometheus scaling triggers on custom metrics such as business metrics or SLO indicators. Its metadata includes serverAddress, metricName, query (PromQL) and threshold; desired replicas = query value ÷ threshold.

questions.q: A team must choose a scaler for an Azure Storage Queue. A community-maintained scaler and the Azure-native one can both read the queue. Which does Learn recommend, and why?

options.text: Either one, because every KEDA scaler has the same support level
options.why: Scalers are categorized by maintainer, and their support differs.

options.text: The community scaler, because open-source scalers get updates faster
options.why: Learn doesn't make that claim. It notes that community scalers can vary in documentation and support.

options.text: The Azure-native scaler, which Microsoft maintains with first-party support
options.why: Correct. Start with Azure-native scalers for Azure resources; community scalers can have varying documentation and support.

options.text: An external scaler, because it runs as a separate component
options.why: External scalers need a separately deployed component, which adds work and isn't needed here.

questions.hint: Scalers are grouped by who maintains them. Which group gets first-party support for Azure resources?
questions.explain: Microsoft maintains Azure-native scalers (Service Bus, Event Hubs, Storage Queue, Blob, Log Analytics, Azure Monitor). Community-maintained scalers vary in documentation and support. External scalers run as separate components.

questions.q: You allocate 0.5 CPU cores to a container. What is the minimum memory you must allocate?

options.text: 2.0 GiB
options.why: That's more than required.

options.text: 4.0 GiB
options.why: That's far more than required.

options.text: 0.5 GiB
options.why: Memory must be at least twice the CPU value.

options.text: 1.0 GiB
options.why: Correct. 2 × 0.5 = 1.0 GiB.

questions.hint: There's a fixed ratio between memory in GiB and CPU in cores.
questions.explain: Memory in GiB must be at least twice the CPU in cores.

questions.q: An inference container needs a GPU and 12 GiB of memory. Which environment option does Learn require?

options.text: A Consumption-only environment
options.why: Consumption maxes out at 4 cores and 8 GiB per container and has no GPU.

options.text: The Consumption profile in a workload profiles environment
options.why: The Consumption profile has the same limits as Consumption-only.

options.text: A Dedicated workload profile
options.why: Correct. Dedicated profiles are required for GPU workloads and allocations above 4 cores or 8 GiB.

options.text: Two containers of 6 GiB each in the Consumption plan
options.why: The requirement is per container, and the GPU need remains.

questions.hint: GPUs and bigger allocations aren't available in the serverless profile.
questions.explain: Dedicated workload profiles support GPU, larger allocations and consistent performance.

questions.q: A container app has a main inference container and a logging sidecar. The inference container needs 6 cores and 12 GiB. The app runs in a Consumption-only environment. What happens?

options.text: It doesn't fit: Consumption allows up to 4 cores and 8 GiB per container, so it needs a Dedicated workload profile
options.why: Correct. The Consumption limit applies per container, and larger allocations need a Dedicated profile.

options.text: It fits, because the limit applies to the whole replica and the sidecar is small
options.why: The 4-core / 8-GiB limit is per container, not per replica.

options.text: It fits once the memory is raised to 24 GiB to keep the 2:1 ratio
options.why: The ratio doesn't lift the per-container limit in Consumption.

options.text: It fits if you raise --max-replicas so that the load spreads
options.why: More replicas don't change the limit for one container's allocation.

questions.hint: The Consumption plan has a maximum per container. Does it apply per container or per replica?
questions.explain: In the Consumption plan, the maximum allocation per container is 4 cores and 8 GiB, applied per container (not per replica). Larger allocations or GPUs need a Dedicated workload profile.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. An app uses 0.5 cores and 1.0 GiB per replica with `--max-replicas 20` in the Consumption plan.

rows.text: At peak, the app can use up to 10 cores of processing capacity.
If a replica exceeds its CPU allocation, the platform terminates and restarts it.
rows.why: CPU over-use is throttled; exceeding memory causes termination.

rows.text: Running replicas that aren't processing requests are billed at the full active rate.
rows.why: Idle replicas are billed at a lower idle rate.

rows.text: The app could be configured with up to 1000 replicas per revision.
rows.why: The maximum replica count is 1000 per revision.

questions.hint: Capacity is per-replica size times replica count. CPU limits throttle; memory limits restart.
questions.explain: Total capacity = per-replica size × replica count; memory limits restart, CPU limits throttle.

questions.q: Which change to a container app creates a new revision?

options.text: Changing the ingress settings
options.why: Ingress settings are application scope.

options.text: Changing the traffic splitting weights
options.why: Traffic rules are application scope.

options.text: Updating a secret value
options.why: Secrets are application scope; no new revision.

options.text: Changing an environment variable
options.why: Correct. Environment variables are part of the template, so they're revision scope.

questions.hint: Template changes create revisions. Secrets, ingress and traffic rules don't.
questions.explain: Template (revision-scope) changes create revisions; secrets, ingress and traffic rules don't.

questions.q: Testers must reach the new revision through a stable URL before it receives any production traffic, without changing the current 100/0 weights. What should you use?

options.text: A revision label on the new revision
options.why: Correct. A label URL always routes to the labelled revision, independent of traffic splitting.

options.text: Single revision mode
options.why: Single revision mode shifts all traffic to the new revision.

options.text: A traffic weight on latest
options.why: A weight on latest sends production traffic to the new revision.

options.text: A second container app environment
options.why: A separate environment isn't needed; labels solve this directly.

questions.hint: You want a stable URL to one revision that's separate from traffic weights.
questions.explain: Labels give direct access to a revision for testing, separate from traffic splitting.

questions.q: Two revisions each have minReplicas 1 and an HTTP rule, and traffic is split 50/50 for a week. Costs are higher than with one revision, and neither revision scaled up at peak. What explains this?

options.text: Labels on both revisions double the replica count for each request
options.why: Labels don't change replica counts.

options.text: Each revision scales on its own share of traffic and keeps its own minimum
options.why: Correct. Each revision keeps its own minimum and sees only half the traffic, so it may not cross the threshold.

options.text: Traffic splitting disables scale rules until the split returns to 100/0
options.why: Scale rules stay active during splits.

options.text: Inactive revisions keep consuming resources until they are purged
options.why: Both revisions are active; inactive revisions consume no resources.

questions.hint: Each active revision scales on its own share and keeps its own minimum.
questions.explain: Move through traffic percentages quickly and deactivate old revisions promptly to control resources.

questions.q: You configure traffic splitting between the stable revision and a canary in multiple revision mode, with weights of 90 and 5. The command fails. Why?

options.text: The canary needs a label before it can get weight
options.why: Labels give direct URLs for testing. They aren't needed for weights.

options.text: The weights must total 100 percent
options.why: Correct. Traffic weights across active revisions must total 100 percent.

options.text: A canary must start at 10 percent or more
options.why: There's no minimum canary weight. The total is the problem.

options.text: Traffic splitting needs single revision mode
options.why: Single revision mode has one active revision, so it can't split traffic.

questions.hint: Add up the two weights.
questions.explain: Traffic splitting distributes requests across active revisions by percentage weights that total 100 percent. Routing is probabilistic per request.
